full_judgment:
5. Now the moot question is whether a final decree can be drawn up by the Adalat after the expiry of the period of limitation provided in Article 181 of the Limitation Act. The Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 shortly the Ain was amended by the Artha Rin Adalat (Amendment) Ain, 1997 and by this amendment, section 6Ka had been added wherein it is provided that the decree passed by the Adalat be executable by the Artha Rin Adalat. Section 5(4) provides that the Artha Rin Adalat shall be deemed to he a civil Court and the powers and jurisdiction of a civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure will be applicable to the Artha Rin Adalat subject the Ain. Section 5(5) provides that the Artha Rin Adalat shall follow the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure so far as they are not inconsistent with the provisions of the Ain. The Ain does not provide the procedure to try a suit and executed a decree passed by it, and in the absence of any provision for executing the decree, there is no dispute that the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure will apply. 

 9. Under these provisions the judgment-debtor has been given an opportunity to pay the decreetal amount which such period as may be fixed by the Court. If he fails to satisfy the decree, the Adalat may extend the time fixed for payment of mortgaged money if he can satisfy the Adalat the cause for nonpayment of the decreetal amount before a final decree for sale of the mortgaged property is dawn up. Sub-rule (2) is intended for the benefit of the mortgagor. The respondents did not seek extension of time to pay the decreetal amount before the expiry of the time fixed by the Adalat. Under such circumstances, the decree holder Bank ought to have prayed for drawing up the final decree before the expiry of four months from 1st March, 1994. The decree holder-Bank did not assign any reason whatsoever as to why it did not pray for drawing up the final decree after expiry of the time fixed in the preliminary decree or within a period of three years from the date of expiry of the time mentioned in the preliminary decree as per Article 181 of the Limitation Act. 

 10. A preliminary decree for sale of mortgaged property can be enforced only by applying for an order for a final decree in accordance with Order 34 Rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the limitation for such application will be governed by Article 181 of the Limitation Act. Time for an application for a final decree to starts when the right to apply accrues, that is to say, from the date when the default occurred. It is the date which is fixed in the decree which is relevant under this provision. Admittedly the decree-holder did not file the application within 3 years from the date of default. 

 15. Furthermore, apparently the Adalat drew up the final decree long after the expiry of three years. Even if an appeal was to file, it would have been allowed since the final decree was drawn up after the expiry of the period of limitation and in that case, the writ petitioner would have unnecessarily deposited 50% of the decreetal amount. He did not challenge the judgment or the decree of the Adalat on merit and therefore, if he deposited 50% of the decreetal amount, that would serve no purpose. On a combined reading of section 6 and 7, we are of the view that the expression "order" used in section 6 is superfluous in view of the clear language used in section 7 that an appeal lies from judgment and decree, and that no appeal lies from any order passed by the Adalat. Section 6 should be read subject to the provisions of section 7. In the premises, the High Court Division is perfectly justified in quashing the order dated 24th April, 2003 of the Adalat 

 16. On perusal of the materials on record, particularly the preliminary decree and the application for drawing up final decree, we have reason to believe that the concerned staff of the Rupali Bank Limited, Hajaribagh Branch and its lawyers deliberately did not take steps for drawing up the final decree within the period of limitation in collusion with the judgment-debtors so that the preliminary decree render in fructuous being barred by limitation. This is evident from the application made in the Adalat wherein the decree holder made superficial statements without explaining the reasons for not filing it in time. They simply performed a routine work by filing an application after long lapse of time. The Adalat passed a decree for over forty eight lakh with interest at the rate of 21% in February, 1997. We failed to understand why the concerned officials did not take any step for selling the mortgaged property after expiry of four months from the date of passing of the preliminary decree? This fact proved that they in collusion with the judgment debtors allowed the decree to die a natural death so that the decree could not be executed. By reason of this intentional latches huge amount of decreetal money could not have been recovered from the judgment debtors. Thereafter, the decreetal amount with interest should be recovered from those officials who are responsible for the default. Accordingly, we direct the Managing Director, Rupali Bank Limited to hold an enquiry into the matter and if it is detected that the concerned officials intentionally did not take step for drawing up the final decree with a view to give undue advantage to the judgment-debtors, recover the decreetal amount with interest from them.
